metadata.title: Measurements of performance gaps are sensitive to the level of test stakes: Evidence from PISA and a Field Experiment

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The paper uses PISA 2015 microdata to compute group-level engagement indicators (skip and rapid-guess proportions) and to compare minority/majority groups across the United States, Israel, and Europe. For the PISA analyses, the author explicitly states that observations are weighted using PISA senate weights, which are designed to make estimates representative of the target populations within each country/economy while accounting for the complex sampling design. For the field experiment, the design is a within-subject study of 8th-grade students in selected Israeli schools; the paper does not report the use of PISA-style sampling weights for the experimental regressions. The author also reports robustness checks using entropy balancing to reweight the experimental sample to match national assessment composition, indicating additional weighting for comparability rather than survey representativeness.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study’s main empirical outcomes are (i) engagement proxies in PISA (skipped and rapidly guessed items) and (ii) grade differences between low- and high-stakes mathematics tests in a field experiment. These dependent variables are not reported as PV-based cognitive achievement scores, so PV handling is not applicable. The paper does not describe a missing-data strategy for the analytic samples (e.g., how missing covariates or incomplete responses were handled), beyond specific exclusions reported for PISA group definitions and for outliers in the experiment; this is a reporting gap for missingness handling.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: PISA 2015: the author uses the PISA math test and constructs engagement measures from response time and item responses, excluding specific groups to ensure representativeness (Israel: exclude Ultra-Orthodox and 'Jewish Other'; United States: exclude students who did not report ethnicity or marked 'Other'; Europe: exclude cases without immigration background). The PISA engagement analysis further excludes items not reached (so only items seen are considered for skip/guess rates). Field experiment: conducted in spring 2017 in northern Israel with 8th-grade students from seven Jewish/Arab schools; students were assigned to take both a low-stakes and a naturally high-stakes math test (within-subject). The analysis excludes outliers defined as students whose low-stakes grade exceeds their high-stakes grade by more than 50 points, and excludes two participating Arab schools due to protocol issues (one where the low-stakes test became high-stakes; one where the high-stakes test occurred during Ramadan).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Mathematics (15-year-olds, engagement via skipped + rapid-guess items)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (descriptive group differences; Fig. 1 proportions; weighted by PISA senate weights).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Mathematics the study leveraged Arab ethnicity (vs Jewish) to compare test-taking engagement measured by the proportion of skipped and rapidly guessed items, finding that minority groups (e.g., Arab students in Israel) skip and guess about twice as much as majority groups. This indicates that low-stakes proficiency comparisons may be confounded by heterogeneous effort, so engagement-sensitive interpretation is needed when benchmarking minority-majority gaps.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported as model metrics; Table 1 reports that percentile differences between minority and majority groups do not meaningfully change after filtering (e.g., Israel Arab vs Jewish percentile differences remain similar).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Mathematics the study leveraged Arab ethnicity (vs Jewish) and applied motivation filtering based on skipped/rapid-guess behavior, finding that minority-majority performance gaps do not meaningfully change after filtering unmotivated students or unengaged items. This indicates that motivation filtering may be insufficient to correct the magnitude of low-stakes underestimation when engagement is correlated with proficiency or is not fully separable into 'fully engaged' vs 'unmotivated' students.

main_findings.dataset_used: Field experiment (Israel, 2017) Grade 8 Mathematics (GEMS format; within-subject low-stakes vs naturally high-stakes)
main_findings.target_variable: Performance gap under low vs high stakes (ΔGrade = High − Low; Arab vs Jewish)
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS (Table 3): Arab coefficient on ΔGrade = 6.40 (SE 1.48), ΔPercentile = 4.57 (SE 1.73), ΔZ-score = 0.18 (SE 0.07); Arab Male: ΔGrade = 3.16 (SE 1.22), ΔPercentile = 1.92 (SE 1.12), ΔZ-score = 0.12 (SE 0.05). Controls: full covariates; Num.Obs. = 577; Adj. R² ≈ 0.040–0.054.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the Grade 8 Mathematics field experiment in Israel (within-subject low-stakes vs naturally high-stakes tests), the study leveraged Arab ethnicity (vs Jewish) and gender-specific ethnicity indicators plus parental education and misunderstanding of stakes to predict the grade difference (High − Low), finding that Arab minority students improve more on the low-stakes-to-high-stakes shift than Jewish students. This indicates that low-stakes assessments can substantially overstate minority-majority proficiency gaps, so policymakers should prefer higher-stakes or engagement-robust measurement when estimating equity gaps.

main_findings.dataset_used: Field experiment (Israel, 2017) Grade 8 Mathematics (within-subject low-stakes vs naturally high-stakes)
main_findings.target_variable: Performance gap under low vs high stakes (ΔGrade) across performance distribution
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported as a single regression metric; reported pattern: significant differences only for above-median high-stakes students; Arab average ΔGrade = 29 points (1.3 SD) and Jewish average ΔGrade = 21 points (0.9 SD).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the Grade 8 Mathematics field experiment in Israel, the study leveraged Arab ethnicity (vs Jewish) to examine heterogeneity across the performance distribution, finding that the low-stakes underestimation is concentrated among above-median students (Arab: 29 points / 1.3 SD; Jewish: 21 points / 0.9 SD). This indicates that equity-gap distortions from low-stakes testing may be most severe for students who are already relatively higher-performing, affecting how interventions should be targeted.

data.outcome_summary: The paper combines PISA 2015 Mathematics observational evidence with a within-subject field experiment in Israel (spring 2017) to test whether low-stakes testing engagement biases minority-majority performance-gap measurements. In PISA 2015, minority groups show higher skip+rapid-guess rates (weighted by PISA senate weights), but motivation filtering based on skipping/rapid guessing does not meaningfully change minority-majority performance gaps (Table 1). In the field experiment (n=599 students; 577 in regressions), students perform better on naturally high-stakes tests; for Arab students, the high-minus-low grade difference is larger than for Jewish students (Table 3: Arab ΔGrade=6.40, ΔZ=0.18), implying that the Jewish–Arab gap would be about 60% smaller under high-stakes measurement (0.38 SD to 0.15 SD). The study uses OLS with wild bootstrap clustered by school and includes controls for parental education and misunderstanding of stakes; it does not train ML models, so no PV handling or ML performance metrics apply. Limitations include non-representative school selection and the fact that motivation filtering relies on strong assumptions about engagement–proficiency correlation.
